New Drone Gods: Cao Fei Follows the Tech to the Provinces Share on Facebook Post Show more sharing options Share on WhatsApp Email Print This Page Share on LinkedIn Pin it Submit to Reddit Post to Tumblr A FEW YEARS AGO, Cao Fei began taking stock of a phenomenon she’d been noticing across China: educated urbanites decamping to the country’s hollowed-out villages and rural areas. This trend bucked a long-prevailing assumption that city life was the population’s main horizon of career advancement and social mobility. “Their parents moved from villages to cities, but now these young people are moving back out,” Cao told me when we met in Milan this past spring. “The promise once made by the city is no longer there.” For almost thirty years, Cao, who lives in Beijing, has made experimental films and interactive installations that draw from the stuff of urban youth culture: cosplay, karaoke, street performance, video games. Cao’s works, which tend to alight on broadly felt social conditions, usually do so by isolating an instance of Homo ludens , whether the displaced romance of a virtual encounter or a shift worker shredding his electric guitar on the factory floor. Having just seen the artist’s major new project at Fondazione Prada, in Milan, and visited her career retrospective at the Kunstmuseum Basel , I was struck by the consistency of two contrasting moods across her practice. On the one hand, there’s a fascination with collective joy and the forms of vernacular invention that aspire to it; on the other, there’s an underlying melancholy that points to the inevitability of isolation, an epistemology of loneliness. Her work suggests that whatever game we might be playing, we aren’t playing it together. Related Elena Filipovic to Lead Kunstmuseum Basel Josef Helferstein Named Director of Kunstmuseum Basel Cao was born in Guangzhou in 1978. That same year, Deng Xiaoping’s reform-minded “second revolution” set China on the path to becoming the world’s export powerhouse. The artist was reared and educated in the Greater Pearl River Delta, a manufacturing, logistics, and technology hub that encompasses Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and megacities like her hometown, and the themes she explores in her work are inseparable from China’s rise as an economic behemoth. In the early 2000s, she gained swift recognition for films portraying the social anxiety and ambition of a generation that came of age during the country’s steroidal modernization sweep. In a satiric short video, Rabid Dogs , 2002, for example, white-collar workers dress upas rapacious canines, clutching Burberry bags in their mouths and traversing cubicles on all fours. Whereas many of Cao’s earlier works drew on the anxieties surrounding urban life, her Prada project, “Dash,” 2026, transports us to a terrain that was, until now, largely latent: the countryside. Sprawled across two floors of the institution are the fruits of the artist’s multiyear research into the “new farmers” movement, a quasi-grassroots cultural phenomenon (spurred by social-media influencers and government policy alike) that refers to the estimated twenty million white-collar workers, returning migrants, entrepreneurs, and food activists who have entered the world of modern agriculture. In hours of video interviews displayed on flat-screen monitors, we meet many of these young, often first-generation farmhands, who operate agricultural drones on their phones while sipping flat whites. Some are former IT workers or academics. Others come via the service industry, like Parichat Veesom, aged thirty-seven, who worked at a 7-Eleven and as a construction worker before taking up rice farming. On the ground floor, in the VR game Dash-180c , 2026, viewers adopt the first-person perspective of a drone, which takes them to an overgrown, tropical, post-human 3D universe ruled by monkeys—more funereal than fun. Nearby is The Birth , 2026, a ziggurat partly woven from bags of fertilizer, enclosing a film installation about the assembly of drones, shot in Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam. Elsewhere, Cao has hung a dense trove of research and archival material: posters advertising Zhang Yimou films, Mao-era propaganda, and a cosmological diagram based on classical Chinese thought. Atop hay bales in one of the exhibition’s rooms rest various high-tech research tomes: Women in Precision Agriculture , for instance. Dash , 2026, the forty-seven-minute, two-channel essay-film at the project’s core, is filled with quiet, almost meditative scenes of machines tilling the land that initially conjure a faux-pastoral aesthetic register. This idyll is soon revealed as a decoy once we meet operators at remote workstations who conduct precision-landing tests in deep-green rice paddies. The film is typical of Cao in its combination of staged scenes with documentary footage—which, when placed together, scramble one’s sense of what’s been scripted and what hasn’t. Slender machines plant seeds in grass, pecking the earth like robotic hens; drones and unmanned tractors spray, fertilize, and irrigate; remote-controlled combines harvest rice and bananas. Sci-fi blends with folklore as shamans stand in fields to anoint the new drone gods. (In one interview included in the show, the farmer Mangkorn Sakdarak shares the story of struggling with a glitchy new drone until a Thai monk came and blessed it.) Despite the interviews and representations of real people in the film, its residual humanism is soon overshadowed by the work’s true protagonist: a particularly elegant red-and-black agricultural drone measuring ten feet across and buzzing above the fields like an enormous mosquito. This airborne cyborg—manufactured by XAG, an agricultural-technology company that also makes autonomous vehicles, sensor systems, and other smart-farming tools—is simultaneously an agent of cultivation and destruction. Observing it, there’s a sense that we are experiencing less the machinic mitigation of human woes than the human capitulation to machinic superiority. The introduction of such drones is partially a response to government priorities: In 2024, China launched the Food Security Law and the Smart Agriculture Action plan, intended to alleviate concerns about food security; it includes state-sponsored efforts to encourage technical training, advanced research, and digitally managed agriculture. In the Dash film and across the Prada show, Cao boldly addresses a critical quandary (one that is underlined by her pairing of romantic and pastoral imagery with posters that once promoted Mao- and Reform-era agricultural mechanization initiatives). How to critique technological solutionism without embracing rural idealization and nostalgia of the kind entangled with nationalism and völkisch thought? And how can one reckon with the disasters of state-driven agricultural policies (during the famine of 1959–61, tens of millions died in China) while preserving sympathy for the collective aspirations promulgated through the posters? The ambiguous moral status of the XAG drone suggests a productive nonanswer to the show’s central political dilemma. THE THEMATIC TERRAIN in “Dash” may be familiar to younger viewers in Europe and the Americas, where back-to-the-land and neo-farmer movements have recently spread, although mostly as lifestyle signaling or as a difficult-to-realize ethical imperative in the post-pandemic era. The project resonates with a vague but broadly felt frustration with urban life, exacerbated by return-to-office mandates and cost-of-living hikes. Cao is also touching on a cluster of related social realities: These include the outrage in China against an institution known as “996” (twelve-hour workdays, six days a week) and trends like tangping —“lying flat,” China’s corollary to dropout culture and “quiet quitting.” Observing it, there’s a sense that we are experiencing less the machinic mitigation of human woes than the human capitulation to machinic superiority. To construct her portraits of youthful generations, Cao isolates characters at the crossroads between modernity and an older way of living, caught between the lives they wanted and the lots they were given—a gap, in a way, that stands for the endless contradictions of contemporary China. This leitmotif was on full display in the artist’s career retrospective, “Testimonies to the Near Future,” at the Kunstmuseum Basel. The show includes her breakout 2006 film Whose Utopia , for which Cao researched and interviewed workers in an OSRAM lightbulb factory. In the resulting work, they act out the lives they wish they had—a would-be ballerina, pop star, or breakdancer performing amid machinery on the factory floor before going back to sorting and assembling lightbulbs. Cao’s fascination with juvenescence is less about “youth” as an idealized sociological category and more about the slippage and overlay between coexistent and contradictory experiences of time. Youth, for Cao, serves as a portal to the future. In this sense, her oeuvre is an almost literal manifestation of William Gibson’s famous observation that the future “is already here,” albeit “not very evenly distributed.” The cyberpunk author was suggesting that our world encompasses multiple temporalities, the experience of which is not uniform; for Cao, this might take the form of a shamanic belief persisting in a hypermodern setting. Indeed, as the Basel retrospective makes clear, Cao has sought across the entirety of her career to recover the future in the past—and, equally, to imagine aspects of lost, squandered, or forgotten time as they endure in the future. She does so, for example, by turning a disused Mao-era Beijing cinema into a site for research and production (her “HX Project,” 2019–20) or by staging actors dancing with a blow-up octopus in an AI-aided e-commerce warehouse ( Asia One , 2018). The out-of-time quality of Cao’s work, like its ambiguity of mood,relates to a subtle aesthetic device that has long puzzled me about her practice: the fact that her images, despite their playful optics, haptic interactivity, and alluring surfaces, deliberately lack puncta. It is impossible to distill an overriding message from one of Cao’s films because they rarely resolve into either allegorical abstraction or documentary specificity. In this way, the artist could be said to be a descendant of Harun Farocki, whose investigations of everyday techne her works occasionally resemble; like Cao, Farocki had an interest in the affective and role-playing dimensions of technologized labor, and made an early study of machine vision. Yet Cao’s projects are less expository than Farocki’s, less resolute in their theses. In her work, we often cycle quickly through hope, nostalgia, despair, and exhilaration—such that, since each affect is fleeting, we emerge fundamentally uncommitted. Cao’s deeper subject here concerns the wagers people make on their futures and, by extension, the ways risk is deferred and abstracted in our gamified, appified, casino-like present. Farocki, who read his Marx closely, predicted a world of labor ever more estranged from its effects. Cao’s twist on this legacy has been her discovery that alienation doesn’t always present itself in obvious ways. Insofar as alienated labor is also self -alienated, its representative stage is no longer the factory line but arenas of productivity that are masked as playful: the multiplayer game, the delivery worker’s app, the pointless pop-up. (Across the works in “Dash,” farming comes to look very much like playing a game.) Cao’s deeper subject here concerns the wagers people make on their futures and, by extension, the ways risk is deferred and abstracted in our gamified, appified, casino-like present. The Basel show traces the roots of Cao’s interest in simulation, as manifested in the parallel realities, generational longing, and everyday social theater experienced by young people during China’s early-2000s boom. In Cosplayers , 2004, an eight-minute single-channel video with accompanying photographs, she records the days of virtual-reality-chasing urban roamers. The series “Hip Hop,” 2003–25, meanwhile, gleefully documents the explosion of a global cultural lingua franca, capturing people dancing outdoors in various cities across the world. Cao’s works bring the joy and the delusion of the crowd ever so closely together. The film on view at the Kunstmuseum that will remain with me the longest is the early i.Mirror , 2007, a 3D quasi-documentary (or “machinima” film) shot by Cao’s avatar China Tracy within the multiuser virtual world Second Life , which debuted in 2003. For about half an hour, we follow Tracy as she explores this nascent universe by flying, teleporting, flirting, and shopping; she walks past LAND FOR SALE signs, spots national flags on empty lots, and observes motorcycles on fire. She befriends and finds romance with another avatar, Hug Yue (in real life, an American man in his sixties). Predating the totalizing capitalism of today’s prediction markets, or the disembodied cam-sex of OnlyFans, i.Mirror captures the hope of something that virtual worlds promised but never delivered: the assurance that “to go virtual is the only way to forget about the real darkness,” as Tracy muses in the film. The last minute of i.Mirror , set to an exhilarating post-rock soundtrack by the Shanghai band Prague, earns the video work a place as one of the most significant of our century. Across a series of jump cuts, we see Tracy’s avatar entering virtual casinos, haunting nightclubs, and spotting avatars as they smoke enormous cigarettes, dance on poles, have sex, roll around the floor, glitch, convulse: It’s a portrait of collective ecstasy. I was reminded, watching this ending, that many of these avatars were animated by real people in real time—meaning that, for a brief historical instant, none of this was make-believe. The delusion came later. Before we sold ourselves out to tech companies, or set fire to the house through online bedlam, there was a hope that some “second life” could solve the problems of our damaged first one. Revisiting Cao’s Second Life experiment nearly twenty years later, the work’s now-lapsed optimism gives it an overwhelming pathos. Today, we understand that the impingement of online fantasy on offline reality has been roundly catastrophic. Rather than liberation and shared pleasure, we have inherited the loneliness that Cao has since identified as the central mood of contemporary life, the main riddle of our supermodernity. Once lauded for her exploration of virtual worlds, the artist has emerged as one of our best documentarians of the real one. Pablo Larios is a Senior Editor of Artforum . He lives in Berlin. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Tran Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist when he went missing in Cambodia View image in fullscreen Tran Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist when he went missing in Cambodia Cambodia Melbourne human rights activist disappears in Cambodia as wife urges Albanese government help Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September Australian Associated Press Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.35 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the federal government to find him and bring him home. Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders. But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety. “My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne. “My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.” Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport. The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training. View image in fullscreen Tran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 September Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025. Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing co-operation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates. Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, has described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam. “Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are long-time human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said. Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll. “It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears. “I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy. “Everything is really uncertain.” The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further. “The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday. The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances. https://www.finanznachrichten.de/nachric.text: Plentisoft: EXLANTIX Provided VIP Shuttle Service at the 35th Economic Forum in Poland, Championing Reliable Mobility in Times of Change Karpacz, Poland--(Newsfile Corp. - September 16, 2026) - From September 8 to 10, the 35th Economic Forum in Poland was held in Karpacz. Chery Group served as the exclusive VIP shuttle partner for the event, with vehicles from EXLANTIX, a brand under EXEED, providing dedicated guest transportation along the Wroclaw-Karpacz route. EXLANTIX also set up a vehicle display at the main venue, the Golebiewski Hotel. EXEED INTERNATIONAL shares this update. Widely recognized as Central and Eastern Europe's largest and most prestigious socio-economic gathering, the 35th Economic Forum in Poland has long served as a premier platform for dialogue among political leaders, ministers, business leaders, and academic luminaries. Each annual session draws over 6,000 participants from some 60 countries, featuring more than 500 specialized events across three intensive days. The Forum's agenda spans macroeconomic strategy, artificial intelligence, sustainable development, and other frontier domains-all of which increasingly shape the direction and pace of transformation across the global automotive industry. Having moved from product introduction and brand awareness-building to active participation in a premier global political-economic discourse platform, EXLANTIX is steadily cementing its position as a meaningful player in the region's upscale mobility ecosystem. In both real-world travel scenarios and the most influential social settings, EXLANTIX is not merely seen-it is experienced, recognized, and positioned as a brand that articulates a clear vision for the future of mobility.
